narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Uruguayan tango developed around 1880 in the poor neighborhoods of Montevideo.

Writer Jorge Luis Borges emphasized its Afro-Montevidean lineage, recalling Vicente Rossi's assertion that tango is 'the son of the Montevidean milonga and the grandson of the habanera.' The form emerged in public dance spaces such as the San Felipe Academy in Montevideo, developing distinct local variations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries before spreading across Argentina and international circuits.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social dance of public halls and working-class neighborhoods, Uruguayan tango serves as a cornerstone of national cultural identity.
Since 2007, Montevideo holds an annual week-long festival to mark the anniversary of 'La Cumparsita,' alongside civic celebrations like Día del Patrimonio.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Uruguayan tango music is closely linked to tango, milonga, vals, and candombe rhythms.
In 1919, Gerardo Matos Rodríguez wrote 'La Cumparsita' in Montevideo.
A rich Río de la Plata soundscape driven by tango compositions, milonga accents, poetic vocal delivery, and underlying Afro-Uruguayan candombe rhythmic influences.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historic dance venues included public warehouses such as the San Felipe Academy in Montevideo.
Today, performance and practice occur in cultural sites, public plazas like the Torre Telecomunicaciones, and specialized venues such as the Tango Museum of Montevideo located inside Palacio Salvo.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent figures include composer Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, bandleader Francisco Canaro, musicians Manuel Campoamor and Enrique Saborido, lyricist Horacio Ferrer, singers Carlos Gardel, Malena Muyala, and Julio Sosa ('El Varón del Tango'), and the group Bajofondo.
A variety of styles developed across different neighborhoods of Montevideo during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, forming dance styles distinct from those developed in Buenos Aires.
Rooted in Afro-Montevidean musical culture, the dance descended from the Montevidean milonga and habanera, sharing historical development with candombe and traditional Río de la Plata tango.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Uruguayan tango is parent of Milonga: Cited by Rossi and Borges as a direct predecessor ('child of the Montevidean milonga').
Uruguayan tango is influence of Candombe: Afro-Uruguayan rhythm and dance form sharing historical and musical ties in Montevideo.
